Rancid

/RAN-sid/ - the stress falls on RAN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Rancid means spoiled, with the unpleasant taste or smell of fats or oils gone bad.

One rancid walnut can spoil a whole batch of brownies — the oil turns long before the shell shows a thing.

Worked Example

Roman dealers graded olive oil the way sommeliers grade wine, and their manuals are plain about the failure mode: oil stored warm, or pressed from bruised fruit, went sharp and soapy within the year. It was not sold as food after that. Lamp oil fetched a third of the price, and the phrase for a merchant's worst season was a cellar full of lamps.

Rancid is the exact word for that oil, because it means spoiled, with an unpleasant taste or smell — and English reserves it almost entirely for fats: butter, nut oils, frying grease, the crumbs at the bottom of a cracker box. Stale is flat; sour is milk beginning to turn. Rancid is fat chemistry gone over into bitterness, and one bite tells you.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

spoiled: gone bad — any food at all; rancid is specifically fats and oils turned

stale: flavor faded and flat, nothing chemically turned yet

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fresh: just made or just opened

pure: untainted

Where it sits · how far the spoiling has gone — stale → sour → rancid

stale vs. rancid: Stale is the first slide — the flavor has simply faded and gone flat.

sour vs. rancid: Sour goes further than stale — the tang of milk starting to turn — but rancid claims the most: fat fully gone over, sharp and bitter on the tongue.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ranc

Root — ranc: to stink, be spoiled (Latin rancere)

Suffix — -id

Suffix — -id: adjective ending: in a given state

Put it together

Put it together: Ranc- (spoiled, stinking) + -id (in that state) = in a spoiled state. Latin rancere named exactly this souring of fats, and English has kept the word narrow: rancid rarely strays from butter, oil, and grease — the failures you taste before you can name them.

Why there's no new relative to spot

Why there's no new relative to spot: Latin rancere, "to be spoiled through," left behind exactly one other common English word: rancor, bitterness nursed so long it turns — a word you will meet later in this course. Same root, same chemistry of keeping a thing too long; no third relative survives to quiz you on.

Strength Check

Word Choice

concrete / kitchen and chemistry

Rancid is a specialist: fats and oils that have chemically turned — butter, nuts, fryer grease. Sour milk and putrid meat each take their own word, and this unit supplies the set: putrid for decay, fetid for standing air and water, noisome for broad offense. If there is no fat in the story, rancid is the wrong tool.
